questions.title: Amino acid essential under growth/surgical-recovery stress
questions.question: A young child is in an automobile accident that requires surgical intervention and substantial recovery time in the hospital. A consultation with a nutritionist results in a specific dietary plan. The plan included the supplementation of an amino acid that is typically considered a nonessential amino acid. Which of the following amino acids is an essential amino acid under conditions of enhanced growth or surgical recovery?

explanations.A: Correct. Arginine is ordinarily classed as a nonessential amino acid, since the body's own synthetic pathways normally keep pace with demand. Under states of rapid growth or the catabolic stress of surgery and recovery, that demand rises sharply -- arginine feeds directly into protein synthesis, the urea cycle and wound healing -- and the body's own synthesis can no longer keep up, making it conditionally essential and worth supplementing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Serine remains nonessential even under growth or surgical stress; it is not the amino acid this scenario's dietary plan is built around.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Alanine is readily synthesised from pyruvate by transamination and stays nonessential in this same clinical setting; it is not the conditionally essential amino acid the nutritionist is supplementing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glycine is one of the amino acids the body synthesises most easily and does not become conditionally essential under growth or surgical stress the way arginine does.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Tyrosine is synthesised from phenylalanine and remains nonessential as long as phenylalanine intake is adequate; it is not the amino acid this stress-related supplementation scenario is describing.

questions.learning_objective: Identify arginine as the conditionally essential amino acid under growth or surgical-recovery stress.

questions.title: Alpha-helix hydrogen bonding
questions.question: Which of the following characterize alpha-helix regions of proteins?

options.A: They all have the same primary structure
options.B: They require a high content of proline and glycine
options.C: They are formed by hydrogen bonding between two adjacent amino acids in the primary sequence
options.D: They are formed principally by hydrogen bonds between a carbonyl oxygen atom in one peptide bond and the amide hydrogen from a different peptide bond
options.E: They are formed principally by hydrogen bonds between a carbonyl atom in one peptide bond and the hydrogen atoms on the side chain of another amino acid

explanations.A: Incorrect. Different alpha-helical regions, even within the same protein or across different proteins, do not share a single fixed primary (amino acid sequence) structure -- the alpha-helix is a geometry any sequence with a suitable composition can adopt, not a marker of one particular sequence.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the actual relationship: a high content of proline (whose backbone geometry and lack of a free amide hydrogen disrupt the regular hydrogen-bonding pattern) and excess glycine (too flexible) instead destabilises an alpha-helix, rather than being required for one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The alpha-helix's hydrogen bonds do not form between two amino acids immediately adjacent in the primary sequence; they form between backbone atoms of peptide bonds separated by about four residues further along the chain.
explanations.D: Correct. The alpha-helix is held together by hydrogen bonds between the backbone carbonyl oxygen atom of one peptide bond and the backbone amide (N-H) hydrogen of a different peptide bond, about four residues further along the same chain. The repetition of this bonding pattern along the chain's length is what coils it into the helix's regular shape.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The alpha-helix's stabilising hydrogen bonds involve backbone atoms on both sides (carbonyl oxygen and amide hydrogen), not a side chain -- side-chain hydrogen bonding is a separate, tertiary-structure phenomenon, not what defines this secondary structure.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the alpha-helix's hydrogen bonds run between the backbone carbonyl oxygen of one peptide bond and the backbone amide hydrogen of a different peptide bond.

questions.title: Sulphur-containing amino acid
questions.question: Which of the following is a sulphur-containing amino acid?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Histidine's side chain is an imidazole ring, giving it basic character; it carries no sulphur and is not one of the sulphur-containing amino acids.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Proline's side chain cyclises back onto its own backbone nitrogen, giving it a unique ring structure among the amino acids, but that ring contains no sulphur.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leucine's side chain is a simple branched aliphatic hydrocarbon with no sulphur atom; it is a neutral, nonpolar amino acid, not a sulphur-containing one.
explanations.D: Correct. Methionine's side chain ends in a thioether (-S-CH3), making it, alongside cysteine, one of only two sulphur-containing amino acids among the twenty standard ones. Methionine additionally initiates every new polypeptide chain and, once activated to S-adenosylmethionine, serves as the cell's principal methyl-group donor.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Tryptophan's side chain is an indole ring, an aromatic, nitrogen-containing heterocycle; it carries no sulphur and is not a sulphur-containing amino acid.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify methionine as a sulphur-containing amino acid.

questions.title: Alzheimer plaque protein structure
questions.question: Autopsies of patients with Alzheimer's disease show protein aggregates called neurofibrillary tangles and neuritic plaques in various regions of the brain. These plaques exhibit the characteristic staining of amyloid. Which of the following structural features is the most likely characteristic of at least one protein in these plaques?

options.A: A high content of beta-pleated sheet structure
options.B: Disulfide bond crosslinks between polypeptide chains
options.C: A high content of alpha-helical structure
options.E: A high content of random coils

explanations.A: Correct. Amyloid deposits, whatever the underlying disease or precursor protein, share a common misfolded structure: a high content of beta-pleated sheet. This is exactly what gives amyloid its characteristic Congo-red staining and its resistance to normal proteolytic clearance, and it is why the plaques in this vignette stain as amyloid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Disulfide crosslinks are a form of tertiary/quaternary stabilisation seen in many normally folded, secreted proteins, but they are not the structural feature that defines amyloid or that these plaques are being described by.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Amyloid formation is specifically a shift toward beta-pleated sheet, not alpha-helical structure; a high alpha-helical content would describe a differently folded (and non-amyloid) protein.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Amyloid is a misfolded, pathological aggregate, not the protein's normal low-energy native conformation -- the whole clinical significance of amyloid is that the protein has left its native fold behind.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Random coil describes an unstructured, disordered polypeptide with no regular secondary structure, which is the opposite of amyloid's highly ordered, repetitive beta-pleated-sheet stacking.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that amyloid deposits, including Alzheimer's neuritic plaques, share a high content of beta-pleated sheet structure.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: A high content of B-pleated sheet structure", p4

questions.title: Proteasome inhibitor spares which protein class
questions.question: A patient with multiple myeloma has not responded to numerous treatments and his disease is progressing. His oncologist wants to start him on the drug bortezomib. Bortezomib inhibits the proteasome from degrading proteins. Which class of intracellular proteins will be specifically spared from degradation as a result of taking this drug?

explanations.A: Correct. Proteins are tagged for proteasomal destruction by attachment of a polyubiquitin chain, which the 26S proteasome recognises before unfolding and degrading the tagged protein in an ATP-dependent process. Bortezomib inhibits the proteasome's own catalytic activity, so exactly this class -- proteins carrying a polyubiquitin tag -- is specifically spared from the degradation it would otherwise undergo, which is exploited therapeutically in myeloma cells that depend heavily on this pathway to clear excess immunoglobulin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. PEST-sequence proteins are also degraded via ubiquitin-dependent and some ubiquitin-independent proteasomal routes, but the class this question specifically tests, matching the printed key, is the polyubiquitinated proteins that are the proteasome's core substrate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Amyloid proteins are characteristically resistant to normal proteolytic clearance in the first place, including by the proteasome, so bortezomib's inhibition of the proteasome does not meaningfully change their already-poor degradation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Immunoglobulin heavy chains that are misfolded or excess are themselves often degraded via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, but they are not the specific class this vignette and its printed key are naming.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Immunoglobulin light chains, likewise, may be substrates for proteasomal degradation, but the option the printed key identifies as specifically spared is the broader polyubiquitinated-protein class, not light chains specifically.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that bortezomib's inhibition of the proteasome specifically spares polyubiquitinated proteins from degradation.

questions.title: Negative acute-phase reactant
questions.question: All of the following are POSITIVE acute phase reactants EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception. C-reactive protein (CRP) is a classic positive acute-phase reactant, rising sharply during systemic inflammation, so it is not the exception this question asks for.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception. Haptoglobin also rises as a positive acute-phase reactant during inflammation, supporting the general pattern rather than being the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception. Transferrin is usually described in this bank's answer key as behaving with the positive reactants in this list; it is not the option the key marks as the exception here.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception. Alpha-1 antitrypsin rises during the acute-phase response along with CRP and haptoglobin, again fitting the general rising pattern rather than being the exception.
explanations.E: Correct. Albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant: its hepatic synthesis is down-regulated during systemic inflammation, partly to redirect synthetic capacity toward the positive reactants, so its plasma concentration falls rather than rises. It is the one protein in this list that moves in the opposite direction from the rest, making it the exception.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify albumin as a negative acute-phase reactant, in contrast to the positive reactants CRP, haptoglobin and alpha-1 antitrypsin.
questions.module_subject: AUN-CBF-103 > Biochemistry > Amino Acids and Proteins

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Albumin", p5

questions.title: Effect not seen with protein denaturation
questions.question: Which of the following does NOT occur with denaturation of a protein?

explanations.A: Correct, as the exception. Denaturation does NOT decrease viscosity -- it increases it, since an unfolded or aggregated polypeptide occupies a larger, more irregular hydrodynamic volume than the compact native fold did. This is the one property in this list that moves opposite to what an intuitive guess based on 'the protein has come apart' might suggest.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception. Decreased diffusibility genuinely does occur with denaturation, as unfolded or aggregated protein moves less freely through solution -- this option describes a real effect, not the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception. Increased viscosity is exactly what does occur with denaturation, so this option describes a real effect and is not the one the question is asking for.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception. Decreased solubility genuinely occurs, since denaturation exposes hydrophobic residues normally buried in the folded interior, driving aggregation and reduced solubility -- a real effect, not the exception.
explanations.E: Incorrect as the exception. Decreased biological activity genuinely occurs, since a protein's function depends on its precise native fold, which denaturation destroys -- again a real effect, not the exception.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify that protein denaturation increases, rather than decreases, viscosity.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Decreased viscosity", p6

questions.title: Endoplasmic reticulum function
questions.question: The endoplasmic reticulum functions to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Generating the cell's power (ATP) is the mitochondrion's role, not the endoplasmic reticulum's -- the ER is not described as a power-generating unit.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Destroying old or damaged cell parts is chiefly the lysosome's role (and, for whole organelles, autophagy), not a function the endoplasmic reticulum performs.
explanations.C: Correct. The endoplasmic reticulum synthesises proteins on its rough (ribosome-studded) portion and lipids on its smooth portion. Proteins made here are then packaged into transport vesicles and sent onward to the Golgi body for further processing and export.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Housing oxidative enzymes for reactive-oxygen and fatty-acid metabolism is characteristic of the peroxisome, not the endoplasmic reticulum.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify protein synthesis as a function of the endoplasmic reticulum.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: synthesize proteins", p8

questions.title: Organelle that packages and exports proteins
questions.question: This organelle packages proteins for the cell and sends them out of the cell to other cells:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis itself (translation), not the organelle that packages finished proteins for export.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The endoplasmic reticulum synthesises the proteins in the first place and sends them onward, but the packaging-and-export role this question asks about belongs to the organelle that receives the ER's output next.
explanations.C: Correct. The Golgi body (Golgi apparatus) receives proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, further modifies and sorts them, and packages them into vesicles for export out of the cell (secretion) or delivery to the plasma membrane or other organelles. Its stacked, flattened sacs process cargo in a fixed cis-to-trans sequence, so material leaving the trans face is already sorted for its final destination.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lysosome is the organelle responsible for intracellular digestion and degradation, not for packaging proteins for export to other cells.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify the Golgi body as the organelle that packages proteins and exports them out of the cell.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Golgi body", p9

questions.title: General definition of vitamins
questions.question: Vitamins are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vitamins are chemically diverse organic compounds, not proteins -- their classification is unrelated to the protein class entirely.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vitamins are diet-derived, not products of the body's own endocrine glands; that description instead fits hormones, a functionally different class of regulatory molecule.
explanations.C: Correct. Vitamins are accessory food factors: organic compounds the body generally cannot synthesise in adequate amounts, needed in small quantities from the diet to support normal growth and metabolism. They function chiefly as coenzymes for specific metabolic enzymes, or, for the fat-soluble vitamins, in specialised regulatory and structural roles.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This is essentially the opposite of what defines a vitamin -- vitamins are, by definition, compounds the body cannot generally synthesise in adequate amounts, which is exactly why they must be obtained from the diet.

questions.learning_objective: Define vitamins as accessory food factors.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Accessory food factors", p11

questions.title: Vitamin required for hydroxyproline formation
questions.question: The vitamin required for the formation of hydroxyproline (in collagen) is:

explanations.A: Correct. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is the cofactor required by prolyl hydroxylase to hydroxylate proline residues into hydroxyproline during collagen synthesis, by keeping the enzyme's catalytic iron centre in its reduced state. Hydroxyproline is essential for collagen's triple-helix stability, and vitamin C's failure to support this step is the direct biochemical basis of scurvy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vitamin E is the body's principal lipid-soluble antioxidant; it plays no role in the enzymatic hydroxylation of proline during collagen synthesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vitamin A's roles are in vision, epithelial maintenance and gene expression; it is not the cofactor for collagen's proline-hydroxylation step.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vitamin D's active form regulates calcium and bone mineralisation; it is unrelated to the hydroxylation reaction that produces hydroxyproline in collagen.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that vitamin C is required for the hydroxylation of proline to hydroxyproline in collagen synthesis.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Vitamin C", p12

questions.title: Pyridoxal phosphate and transamination
questions.question: Pyridoxal phosphate is central to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Carboxylation reactions typically require biotin as their coenzyme, not pyridoxal phosphate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Amidation is not the reaction class pyridoxal phosphate is characteristically associated with; it is not the printed answer for this stem.
explanations.C: Correct. Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the active coenzyme form of vitamin B6, is the coenzyme transaminase enzymes require to shuttle an amino group from one amino acid to a keto-acid acceptor. Transamination is central to both amino acid synthesis and their catabolic entry into central metabolic pathways.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Deamination (removal of an amino group without transfer to another molecule) is a related but distinct reaction from transamination, and is not the reaction this question's printed key names PLP as central to.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that pyridoxal phosphate is the coenzyme central to transamination.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Transamination", p17

questions.title: Vitamin coenzyme for transaminase action
questions.question: The vitamin required as coenzyme for the action of transaminases is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Riboflavin's active coenzyme forms (FAD, FMN) act as hydrogen carriers in oxidation-reduction reactions, not as the transaminase coenzyme.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Niacin's active coenzyme forms (NAD+, NADP+) likewise act as hydrogen/electron carriers, not as the coenzyme transaminases specifically require.
explanations.C: Correct. Pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6, is the specific coenzyme transaminase (aminotransferase) enzymes require for amino-group transfer between an amino acid and a keto-acid acceptor. This transamination reaction is central to both amino acid synthesis and the entry of their carbon skeletons into central catabolic pathways.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pantothenic acid's active form (as part of coenzyme A) functions as an acyl-group carrier, not as the coenzyme for transamination reactions.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify pyridoxal phosphate as the vitamin coenzyme required for transaminase action.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Pyridoxal phosphate", p17

questions.title: Vitamin deficiency linked to infant convulsions
questions.question: Convulsion in human infants has been attributed to the deficiency of the vitamin:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vitamin B12 deficiency classically produces megaloblastic anaemia and, over time, subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, not the convulsions this question is asking about.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency classically produces beriberi and Wernicke's disease, not the infant convulsions this question describes.
explanations.C: Correct. Pyridoxal phosphate (active vitamin B6) is the coenzyme for glutamate decarboxylase, which converts the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate into GABA, the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter of the CNS. Vitamin B6 deficiency impairs this GABA-synthesis step and tips the excitatory/inhibitory balance toward excitation, which is the mechanistic basis of the convulsions vitamin B6 deficiency classically causes, especially in infants.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) deficiency classically produces glossitis, angular stomatitis and corneal vascularisation, not the infant convulsions this question describes.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that vitamin B6 deficiency has been linked to convulsions in infants, via impaired GABA synthesis.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: B6", p17

questions.title: Vitamin B12 corrin ring central metal
questions.question: The central structure of vitamin B12 (the corrin ring system) is centred on:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Iron is the metal at the centre of the structurally related porphyrin (haem) ring, not the corrin ring of vitamin B12 -- a frequently confused pair given how similar the two macrocycles are.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Manganese is not the metal coordinated at the centre of B12's corrin ring; it plays no defining structural role here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Magnesium is the metal at the centre of the chlorophyll (porphyrin-family) ring in plants, not the corrin ring of vitamin B12.
explanations.D: Correct. Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is built around a corrin ring -- a macrocycle related to but distinct from porphyrin -- whose centre coordinates a cobalt atom. Cobalt is what gives cobalamin its name and is essential to both of its coenzyme forms, methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that vitamin B12's corrin ring is centred on cobalt.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Cobalt", p19

questions.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency clinical name
questions.question: A deficiency of vitamin B12 due to loss of intrinsic factor causes:

explanations.A: Correct. When vitamin B12 deficiency is specifically caused by loss of intrinsic factor (most commonly autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells, which produce it), the resulting megaloblastic anaemia is given the specific clinical name pernicious anaemia. This distinguishes it from B12 deficiency caused by simple dietary lack, which produces the same blood picture without the intrinsic-factor cause.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rickets is the childhood presentation of vitamin D deficiency, affecting bone mineralisation, not a presentation of vitamin B12 deficiency.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Scurvy is the clinical name for vitamin C deficiency, affecting collagen synthesis, not vitamin B12 deficiency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Beri-beri is the clinical name for vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency, not vitamin B12 deficiency.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that vitamin B12 deficiency caused by loss of intrinsic factor is specifically termed pernicious anaemia.

questions.title: Urinary marker of vitamin B12 deficiency
questions.question: Vitamin B12 deficiency can be diagnosed by urinary excretion of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Raised urinary lactate reflects anaerobic glycolysis or lactic acidosis, not the specific enzymatic block that defines vitamin B12 deficiency.
explanations.B: Correct. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is one of only two human enzymes requiring a vitamin B12 coenzyme (adenosylcobalamin). When B12 is deficient, methylmalonyl-CoA accumulates and is converted to methylmalonic acid, so raised urinary (or serum) methylmalonate is a specific diagnostic marker of B12 deficiency. Folate deficiency, which produces the identical megaloblastic blood picture, does not share this marker, which is why it is used to tell the two apart.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Malate is a citric acid cycle intermediate whose urinary excretion is not the marker vitamin B12 deficiency is diagnosed by.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pyruvate is the end-product of glycolysis and is not the urinary marker specific to vitamin B12 deficiency.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that raised urinary methylmalonate is a specific diagnostic marker of vitamin B12 deficiency.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Methylmalonate", p20

questions.title: Chemical structure of folate
questions.question: Folic acid (folate) consists of:

options.A: A pteridine base, para-aminobenzoic acid and glutamate
options.B: A pteridine base, para-aminobenzoic acid and aspartate
options.C: A purine base, para-aminobenzoic acid and glutamate
options.D: A purine base, para-hydroxybenzoic acid and glutamate

explanations.A: Correct. Folate (folic acid) is structurally a pteridine ring joined to para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), which is in turn joined to one or more glutamate residues. This pteridine-PABA-glutamate combination is folate's defining structure, distinct from the purine bases used elsewhere in nucleotide metabolism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Folate's third component is glutamate, not aspartate; substituting aspartate misstates the actual structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Folate's base ring is a pteridine, not a purine -- pteridine and purine are related but distinct heterocyclic ring systems, and this option substitutes the wrong one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This option combines two errors: folate's base is a pteridine, not a purine, and its middle component is para-aminobenzoic acid, not para-hydroxybenzoic acid.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that folate is built from a pteridine base, para-aminobenzoic acid and glutamate.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Base pteridine, p-amino benzoic acid and glutamate", p21
